title: USAA's Florida Return: A $500 Million Dividend to About 830,000 Members as Part of Nearly $1 Billion in Rate Cuts and Payouts
summary: USAA says it is paying a $500 million dividend to about 830,000 Florida auto members from June 15, 2026, with rate cuts averaging 14% and an earlier $160 million dividend, crediting Florida's tort reforms, in a broader effort that includes lower rates nationally.
description:
One of America's largest military-focused insurers is sending money back to its Florida customers. USAA announced on June 8, 2026 that it will pay a $500 million dividend to about 830,000 Florida auto members, starting on June 15, as part of a package of rate reductions and payments that it describes as nearly $1 billion for the state. This article is based on USAA's press release, headlined as a broadening of its national effort to help military families with rising costs, and supplements it with reporting from the trade press. The figures are the company's own and have not been audited by us. An earlier version of this article said the payments were a direct pass-through of tort reform savings and that no claim was required; the release says the dividend goes to eligible members and credits tort reform as a factor, so the wording has been corrected.

First, the details of the Florida programme. USAA says the $500 million dividend goes to about 830,000 members who held USAA auto policies between 2023 and 2025. From June 15, eligible current Florida auto policyholders are expected to receive an average dividend of about $760, and more than a quarter will receive over $1,000. The release also lists two earlier steps. In December 2025, USAA paid $160 million in dividends to eligible members. From January to July 2026, it expects about $250 million in savings from auto rate reductions that average 14%, made through two rate filings. The release describes the Florida actions as totalling nearly $1 billion, between December 2025 and July 2026. The three itemised amounts, $160 million, $250 million and $500 million, add up to $910 million, so the description of nearly $1 billion is rounded up.

Why is USAA doing this? The company says the auto insurance industry raised rates over the past five years because of natural disaster activity, inflation and what it calls legal system abuse, and that it is reversing that trend. It credits Florida's civil litigation and tort reforms with curbing legal system abuse and reducing the legal costs that drove premium increases. Tort reform is the name for changes to the rules about lawsuits. In Florida, reforms in 2022 and 2023 included changes to attorney fee rules and to how fraud and litigation are handled. USAA also says Georgia and Louisiana enacted tort reforms in 2025 and that New York is following suit. Critics of tort reform, such as consumer groups and trial lawyers, argue that limiting lawsuits can reduce the rights of injured people, a debate not covered in the release.

What does it mean beyond Florida? The release says that in 2026 about half of USAA policyholders are expected to see reductions in their six-month auto premiums. It lists other actions: safe-driving programmes called SafePilot and SafePilot Miles, which lower auto premiums based on driving behaviour and mileage, and reductions in or elimination of some banking fees at USAA Bank, along with credit products with competitive rates. Juan Andrade, USAA's president and chief executive, said that as the cost of living rises the company is focused on putting real money back into members' pockets in multiple ways, and that military families already carry enough on their shoulders.

How does this fit the market picture? The wider data show that the US auto insurance market became very profitable in 2025. S&P Global Market Intelligence's analysis of the first quarter of 2026 reported that private passenger auto's direct incurred loss ratio was about 60%, and the USAA group's underwriting results were part of an industry that earned strong profits. When insurers are very profitable and competition is increasing, as Progressive's growth shows, returning money to members through dividends and rate cuts is both a customer benefit and a competitive move. A dividend is different from a rate cut: it is a one-time payment and not a lasting reduction in price, and policyholders should not assume that it will be repeated.

Who is eligible, and what should they do? According to the release, the dividend is for members who held a USAA auto policy in the period from 2023 to 2025, and current policyholders are expected to receive it from June 15. People who are no longer customers or who held policies outside Florida may not qualify, and the exact rules are USAA's. Members should check their USAA account or contact the company for details and watch for official messages, remembering that scammers often imitate such announcements.

For Florida drivers more generally, the lesson is that rates differ by insurer, so comparing quotes remains worthwhile. Several Florida insurers have lowered rates or paid back money in 2026. USAA's service is limited to military members, veterans and their families, so the programme will not reach most residents, but it is a visible sign of the effects of reform on one of the largest auto insurers. USAA was founded in 1922 by a group of military officers, serves more than 14.5 million members, is based in San Antonio, and employs more than 36,000 people.
image_alt: US military auto insurance dividend Florida tort reform savings (illustrative)
key_points: USAA says a $500 million dividend will go to about 830,000 members who held Florida auto policies between 2023 and 2025, starting June 15, 2026, with an average of about $760 and more than a quarter receiving over $1,000.

The Florida actions between December 2025 and July 2026 also include $160 million of dividends in December 2025 and about $250 million in savings from rate reductions averaging 14% through two filings.
The release describes the total as nearly $1 billion, but the three itemised figures add to $910 million.

USAA credits Florida's civil litigation and tort reforms for curbing legal system abuse and says Georgia and Louisiana enacted reforms in 2025 and New York is following; about half of USAA policyholders should see lower six-month auto premiums in 2026.
USAA was founded in 1922, serves more than 14.5 million members and employs more than 36,000 people.
why_it_matters: Florida's tort reforms were designed to cut legal costs that drove up car insurance premiums. A large insurer returning money and cutting rates is the clearest evidence customers have seen of that policy translating into savings, though the figures come from the company itself.

title: Allianz Global Insurance Report 2026: Premiums Reach €6.9 Trillion as Health Grows 12.3% and Asia Is Set to Add the Most Over the Next Decade
summary: Allianz Research says global premiums grew 7.1% in 2025, with health insurance expanding fastest since 2014 and property and casualty growth cooling, and projects about 5.3% a year growth to 2036, led by Asia.
description:
Global insurance is still growing at a healthy pace, but the mix is changing, according to the latest annual assessment from Allianz Research. The Global Insurance Report 2026, published by the research arm of the German insurer Allianz on May 28, 2026, puts total premiums at €6.9 trillion in 2025 and shows that health insurance, not the traditional property and casualty lines, is now the fastest-growing segment. This article summarises the figures published on the Allianz website. An earlier version contained several figures that do not appear on that page, including an insurance penetration ratio and a 2026 world GDP forecast, and they have been removed.

The headline is that global premiums grew 7.1% in 2025, adding €456 billion to the total. That is slower than the exceptional 9.4% growth of 2024, but still above the ten-year compound annual growth rate of 5.6%. Premiums are the payments customers make to insurers, so the total is a measure of the size of the industry, though it is also affected by price changes and exchange rates.

The three main segments grew at very different speeds. Life insurance remained the largest, with premiums of €2,861 billion, up 6.9%, compared with growth of 11.3% in 2024. Property and casualty insurance, which covers homes, vehicles and businesses, reached €2,320 billion, up 3.8%, compared with 8.5% in 2024. Health insurance reached €1,688 billion, up 12.3%, the strongest expansion since 2014. Allianz notes that in health, North America grew 14.9% and that the United States accounts for more than 70% of global health premiums. That means much of the global health figure reflects American medical costs and coverage, a point worth remembering when comparing it with growth in other regions.

The regional detail matters. In property and casualty, North America holds 52% of global premiums, but its growth slowed to 2.2% from 9.7% in 2024. Western Europe grew 5.3% and Asia 4.0%. The slowdown in North America reflects the end of the sharp price increases that followed several years of high claims, and our coverage of US insurers this week shows how profitable the market has become. In life insurance, Asia is the largest market and grew 9.9%, with China up 11.4%. The report notes that health insurance penetration, meaning premiums as a share of the economy, is below 1% in almost all Asian markets, which suggests room for growth.

Looking ahead, Allianz projects that the global market will grow by about 5.3% a year to 2036, slightly faster than the world economy. Property and casualty is expected to grow 4.7% a year, life 4.9% and health 6.7%, the fastest of the three. Over the ten years the global premium pool would expand by about €5,260 billion, made up of €1,991 billion in life, €1,505 billion in property and casualty, 44% of which comes from North America, and €1,764 billion in health, mostly in the United States. By region, wider Asia is expected to add €1,004 billion, more than North America, at €416 billion, and Western Europe, at €402 billion, combined. As a result, North America is expected to hold about 46% of global premiums through 2036, a slight decline of half a percentage point. India and China together should gain almost four percentage points of market share, while Western Europe may lose about four points, after losing 5.3 points over the past decade.

These are projections that depend on assumptions about growth, prices and policy, and they should be read as a central scenario, not a forecast of any single year. A decade is a long time, and the figures could change with the economy, interest rates, regulation or large losses.

The risks Allianz highlights centre on geopolitics. The report says geopolitical fragmentation makes risk environments more complex, challenges cross-border business models and weakens the diversification benefits that large international insurers have relied on. At the same time, it sees opportunities in demand for infrastructure, energy security and political risk insurance. Insurers are advised to build more regionally resilient operating models and to integrate geopolitical analysis into underwriting and capital allocation. In practice this means that a company that spreads risk across many countries may find those countries are exposed to the same shocks, for example in energy supply or trade rules.

What should readers take from this? For customers, the growth in health premiums is a sign of rising medical costs and rising demand for cover, and it points to continued upward pressure on health insurance prices in many markets. For businesses and homeowners, the slowdown in property and casualty growth in North America suggests that the period of steep price rises has ended, although the report does not forecast future price changes. For investors and policymakers, the shift of growth to Asia indicates where new customers will come from, particularly in life and health, where penetration is low.

Two cautions apply. First, premium totals combine real growth in coverage with price effects, so a rise does not necessarily mean more people are insured. Second, the report is one institution's view, and other research houses, such as Swiss Re, publish different estimates using different methods. Readers who want to compare should check the definitions used. The full report on the Allianz website gives the underlying tables and the country detail.
image_alt: Global insurance industry premium growth annual report 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Allianz Research's report of May 28, 2026 puts global insurance premiums at €6.9 trillion in 2025, up 7.1% or €456 billion, after 9.4% in 2024 and above the ten-year average of 5.6%.
Life premiums were €2,861 billion (up 6.9%), property and casualty €2,320 billion (up 3.8%) and health €1,688 billion (up 12.3%, the fastest since 2014).
North America holds 52% of global P&C premiums but its P&C growth slowed to 2.2% from 9.7%; Asian life premiums grew 9.9%, with China up 11.4%.
Allianz projects about 5.3% annual global premium growth to 2036, adding about €5,260 billion, with Asia expected to add €1,004 billion, more than North America and Western Europe combined.
Geopolitical fragmentation is the main risk the report highlights, weakening diversification and complicating cross-border business models.
why_it_matters: Premium totals show where insurance is growing and where it is not. Health is the fastest-growing line, property and casualty is cooling after price rises, and Asia is set to drive the next decade, which shapes where insurers invest and which customers they compete for.

title: Allianz Research: India Is Set to Be the World's Fastest-Growing Major Insurance Market, With Premiums Growing 10.7% a Year Through 2036
summary: Citing the Allianz Global Insurance Report 2026, Business Today reports India's insurance premiums grew 9.4% in 2025 to ₹13.96 lakh crore ($145.9 billion) and are projected to grow 10.7% a year to 2036, with health the fastest segment at 12.5%.
description:
India's insurance market is set to grow faster than that of any other large economy over the next decade, according to Allianz Research. The projection comes from the Allianz Global Insurance Report 2026 and was reported by Business Today on June 3, 2026. This article summarises the figures as reported. An earlier version of this article said the headline of 'tripling by 2036' was in the report and linked growth to a May 2026 foreign investment change. The Business Today article body does not state the tripling, which would be an over-statement of the growth rate, and does not mention foreign investment, so those claims have been removed. At a 10.7% annual rate, premiums would grow by roughly 2.7 times over ten years, which is our own arithmetic and not a figure from the report.

First, the size of the market. India's insurance premium income reached ₹13.96 lakh crore, or US$145.9 billion, in 2025, according to the article. That compares with ₹12.76 lakh crore, or US$133.4 billion, in 2024, which is growth of 9.4%. The article says growth was broad, across life, health and general insurance. For comparison, the global insurance market grew 7.1% in 2025 to US$8.1 trillion, adding US$536 billion, according to the same report as cited, and Allianz expects global growth of 5.3% a year through 2036. India is therefore growing faster than the world average, from a base that is still small relative to the size of its economy.

The forecast is the headline. Allianz projects that Indian premium income will grow at an average annual rate of 10.7% through 2036, and it expects India to be the fastest-growing major insurance market in the world over the coming decade. The projection is a central scenario that depends on assumptions about the economy, regulation and consumer demand. A decade is a long horizon, and changes in interest rates, claims experience or policy could move the outcome.

The segments tell different stories. Life insurance is the dominant line, accounting for about 74% of total premium income. It grew 9.7% in 2025 and is projected to grow 10.5% a year through 2036. Health insurance is smaller but faster. Its premiums grew 10.4% in 2025, the strongest performance of the year according to the article, and Allianz expects it to be the fastest-growing segment, with growth of 12.5% a year over the next decade. The article does not give separate figures for general insurance, which covers motor, property and similar lines.

Why is there room for so much growth? Because many Indians are still not covered. Insurance penetration, which is premiums as a share of gross domestic product, is 3.8% of GDP, according to the article. That is low compared with many developed markets, though the report as quoted does not give specific comparisons, and the penetration of life insurance differs from non-life. The article also says that about 46% of India's working-age population is effectively covered by pension systems, and that a large share of healthcare spending is funded directly by households out of pocket. Out-of-pocket spending is a sign of unmet demand for health insurance, because a medical emergency can force families into debt.

The drivers cited are rising incomes, greater awareness of financial protection, healthcare inflation, regulatory reforms, digital adoption and product innovation. The article also refers to the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India's vision of insurance for all by 2047, which aims to widen coverage, make it more affordable and improve operational efficiency. Our own reporting on the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, which raised the limit on foreign ownership of Indian insurers from 74% to 100%, shows one of the regulatory reforms that may support investment, though the Allianz coverage as reported does not mention it.

What does this mean for consumers? First, more competition and more product choice should in time benefit buyers, but the growth of health insurance also reflects rising medical costs, which tend to push premiums up. Second, because health insurance is becoming the fastest-growing area, consumers should read policy terms carefully, including sub-limits, waiting periods and exclusions, and compare claim settlement records. Third, low penetration means many households may remain underinsured, so basic protection, such as term life and a health cover with adequate sum insured, deserves priority.

For insurers and investors, a market that grows at 10% or more a year offers opportunities but also challenges. Rapid growth needs capital, distribution and technology, and it can bring pressure on margins and conduct. Company results in India, such as those of HDFC Life and ICICI Life, show how growth and profitability balance in practice, with attention on value of new business and persistency, meaning how many customers keep paying premiums.

This article reports a forecast and should not be read as a guarantee. Readers who want the underlying numbers and the methodology should consult the Allianz Global Insurance Report 2026 itself.
image_alt: India insurance market growth fastest-growing major market 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Allianz Research's Global Insurance Report 2026, as reported on June 3, puts India's 2025 premium income at ₹13.96 lakh crore (US$145.9 billion), up 9.4% from ₹12.76 lakh crore (US$133.4 billion).
Allianz expects India to be the fastest-growing major insurance market in the world, with premiums growing 10.7% a year on average through 2036.
Life insurance is about 74% of premium income, grew 9.7% in 2025 and is projected to grow 10.5% a year; health premiums grew 10.4% in 2025 and are projected to grow 12.5% a year.
Insurance penetration is 3.8% of GDP, about 46% of the working-age population is effectively covered by pension systems, and much healthcare spending is paid out of pocket.
Cited growth drivers include rising incomes, awareness, healthcare inflation, regulatory reform, digital adoption and product innovation, alongside IRDAI's 'Insurance for All by 2047' vision.
why_it_matters: India combines a large population, low insurance penetration and rapid growth, which makes it a priority market for insurers and investors. For households, it shows how much protection is still unpaid for and how health cover is becoming the main growth area.

title: Fitch Keeps Its Asia-Pacific Insurance Outlook Neutral for 2026 but Rates China and Taiwan Life as Deteriorating
summary: Fitch's June 9 report holds a neutral 2026 outlook for Asia-Pacific insurance, with only China life and Taiwan life rated deteriorating, as new solvency regimes in Japan, Taiwan and Indonesia and rising claims costs offset strong capital buffers.
description:
Fitch Ratings expects 2026 to be a steady but not spectacular year for insurers in the Asia-Pacific region. In a report dated June 9, 2026 and covered by Insurance Business Asia on June 12, the agency maintained a neutral sector outlook for most of the region and flagged just two segments, life insurance in China and in Taiwan, as deteriorating. This article summarises that coverage. An earlier version of this article said that about 92% of insurers rated by Fitch had stable individual outlooks. The article does not give that figure, and states only that two segments are assigned a non-neutral outlook, so the claim has been removed.

What does neutral mean? Fitch's sector outlooks assess the direction of fundamentals over the coming year. Neutral means it expects conditions to stay broadly as they are. The agency explains that the outlook reflects offsetting factors. On the positive side are strong capital buffers, disciplined underwriting and better management of assets and liabilities. On the negative side are rising claims costs, modest inflation, and newly implemented solvency regimes that change how capital is measured.

In non-life insurance, such as motor, property and health, Fitch says underwriting margins are narrowing as loss ratios rise. Supply-chain disruption tied to geopolitical tensions is adding to claims costs, because repair parts and materials cost more. The report picks out specific markets: Korea and Indonesia are seeing higher health and motor losses, and in Australia home and vehicle repair costs remain high. There are offsets, including higher interest rates, which raise investment income, more favourable reinsurance terms, and earlier rate increases that are still earning through. Fitch lists late-cycle market conditions and credit risk as the downside risks.

Japan is a case study in regulatory change. The country's new economic value-based solvency framework took effect at the end of March 2026. Under such a framework, insurers' assets and liabilities are valued at market-consistent levels, which makes the solvency ratio more sensitive to movements in interest rates and markets than under the old regime. Fitch says insurers are adapting by using retained earnings, issuing hybrid securities and reducing balance sheet risk, and that non-life groups are selling strategic equity stakes, the cross-holdings in other companies that Japanese firms have long held. Fitch says domestic profitability remains stable. This ties into the wave of overseas deals by Japanese insurers, including the Berkshire Hathaway stake in Tokio Marine that we cover in this series.

Indonesia faces a different challenge. A first phase of higher equity requirements for insurers is in effect, and an end-2026 threshold is approaching. Fitch says about 80% of insurers have already met the end-2026 threshold, and smaller insurers that cannot meet the higher thresholds may consolidate. A new accounting standard, PSAK 117, could reduce reported equity at some insurers. Fitch expects stronger market discipline over the medium term.

The two segments with a deteriorating outlook are both life insurance. In China, low domestic interest rates have raised required reserves and capital requirements. A growing allocation to equities makes insurers more sensitive to market swings, and geopolitical risk adds volatility. Insurers are shifting towards participating products, in which customers share in investment returns and the insurer promises less, and are tightening commission controls. Allianz data cited in the article show that Chinese life premiums grew 11.4% in 2025, so the deteriorating outlook relates to profitability and capital, not demand.

In Taiwan, the issue is currency. The sector has significant currency risk because many policies are denominated in US dollars and are interest-sensitive. Accounting changes in 2026 reduce the reported impact of currency moves, but Fitch says this addresses presentation, not the underlying exposure. It also notes that the ability of the updated capital framework to maintain solvency under stress has not yet been tested.

The article adds context from the Allianz Global Insurance Report: Asian life premiums grew 9.9% in 2025, and Asia-Pacific property and casualty premiums grew 4.0%, below the global ten-year compound growth of 5.6%. Those figures show a region with strong life insurance demand and slower non-life growth.

What does this mean for readers? For policyholders, the report is about the financial strength of insurers, and a neutral outlook suggests no broad deterioration in companies' ability to pay claims. For investors, the two deteriorating segments carry risks linked to interest rates, currency and regulation. For regulators, the report shows that moving to market-based solvency regimes has side effects, such as asset sales and consolidation. Fitch's views are one agency's opinions, and its individual company ratings can differ from sector outlooks. This article reports the content of the coverage and not the full report, which is available to Fitch subscribers. Readers comparing markets should also remember that sector outlooks are broad judgements: a neutral outlook can sit alongside weak individual companies, and a deteriorating outlook does not mean every insurer in that market is in difficulty. Watching solvency disclosures, interest rates and currency moves over the coming quarters will show whether Fitch's balance of risks proves right.
image_alt: Asia Pacific insurance sector Fitch ratings outlook 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Fitch's report of June 9, 2026 keeps a neutral 2026 sector outlook for Asia-Pacific insurance, with China life and Taiwan life the only segments rated deteriorating.

Neutral reflects offsetting factors: capital buffers, disciplined underwriting and stronger asset-liability management against rising claims costs, modest inflation and newly implemented solvency regimes.

Japan's value-based economic solvency regime took effect at the end of March 2026 and is more sensitive to markets; insurers are using retained earnings, hybrid securities and lower balance sheet risk, and non-life groups are selling strategic equity stakes.

In Indonesia about 80% of insurers have met the end-2026 equity threshold, and smaller insurers that cannot may consolidate; Taiwan life has significant currency risk from US-dollar interest-sensitive policies.
Non-life margins are narrowing as loss ratios rise, with higher health and motor losses in Korea and Indonesia and high home and vehicle repair costs in Australia.
why_it_matters: Asia-Pacific is where most of the world's future insurance growth is expected. Fitch's view shows which markets are stable, which are under pressure, and how new capital rules are changing behaviour at the largest insurers.

title: Berkshire Hathaway Takes a 2.49% Stake in Tokio Marine for About $1.8 Billion in a 10-Year Reinsurance and Investment Partnership
summary: Berkshire's National Indemnity will buy a 2.49% stake in Tokio Marine Holdings for ¥287.4 billion (about $1.8 billion), alongside a 10-year partnership covering reinsurance and joint investments, with a cap of 9.9% without board approval.
description:
One of the world's best-known investors has taken a stake in Japan's largest property and casualty insurer. On Monday, March 23, 2026, Berkshire Hathaway announced that its subsidiary National Indemnity Company would acquire a 2.49% strategic stake in Tokio Marine Holdings for ¥287.4 billion, about $1.8 billion. The deal comes with a ten-year partnership covering reinsurance and joint investment activity. This article is based on Insurance Journal's report of the announcement. An earlier version said Berkshire's chief executive Greg Abel confirmed at the annual meeting in May that the shares would be held long-term, and called the arrangement a whole-account quota share. Neither statement appears in the report reviewed, so they have been removed.

The terms of the investment are specific. According to the report, Berkshire will buy about $1.8 billion of Tokio Marine's treasury stock, meaning shares the company already holds. Tokio Marine will then buy back the same dollar amount of its existing shares on the market. In effect, the new shares go to Berkshire while the company reduces the number of shares outstanding elsewhere, so the total number held by the public falls. Any further purchases by Berkshire would likely be made on the open market. Berkshire has agreed not to exceed a 9.9% stake without the approval of Tokio Marine's board, a standard protection for the company against an unwelcome increase in influence.

The partnership has several parts. The two companies will collaborate on reinsurance and on global investments, including mergers and acquisitions. Reinsurance is insurance for insurers, in which a company passes part of its risk to another in return for a share of the premium. Tokio Marine can use National Indemnity as a reinsurance option for any type of insurance, without restriction. A Tokio Marine spokesman, Mitsuhiro Izu, said that Berkshire proposed the partnership. The agreement runs for ten years, and for the first five years neither company may enter into similar agreements with competitors, a form of exclusivity that locks in the relationship for a significant period.

Who are the partners? Tokio Marine is Japan's largest property and casualty insurer, with a large international business built through acquisitions over the past two decades. Berkshire Hathaway owns National Indemnity and GEICO, and is among the largest reinsurers in the world. The report notes that Berkshire has been expanding in Japan. Under Warren Buffett it invested in five large Japanese trading houses and said it intended to raise those stakes over time. Late last year Berkshire raised just over ¥210 billion, about $1.3 billion, through yen-denominated bonds, its first Japanese bond issue since 2019. Buffett retired as chief executive at the end of 2025, and Greg Abel succeeded him. Seen against that background, the Tokio Marine investment extends an existing strategy into financial services.

What is in it for each side? For Tokio Marine, the benefits are access to reinsurance capacity from a counterparty with very large capital, a long-term shareholder at a time when many Japanese companies are trying to improve capital efficiency and shareholder returns, and a partner for international acquisitions. The share buyback that accompanies the transaction supports earnings per share. For Berkshire, the stake gives exposure to a leading insurer in a market where interest rates are rising from low levels and where the yen has been weak, and it creates a flow of reinsurance business. The report does not give financial projections for either company, and none should be inferred.

An analyst quoted in the report, Ikuo Mitsui of Aizawa Securities, said the partnership with Berkshire is likely to provide an advantage. That is one opinion, and the report does not say what advantage he expected in the long run.

There are questions that the report does not answer. It does not specify the reinsurance volumes that would be ceded to National Indemnity, the price, or how the joint investment collaboration would work in practice. Nor does it say whether Berkshire has any right to a seat on the board. The 9.9% ceiling and the five-year exclusivity are the main protections described, and observers will watch for details in Tokio Marine's own disclosures and in Berkshire's annual report.

For policyholders in Japan or elsewhere, the direct effects are limited. The arrangement concerns the capital and risk-transfer structure of the insurer and not the terms of customer policies. Indirectly, additional reinsurance capacity could help Tokio Marine write business in markets where catastrophe risk is high, which can support availability of cover.

Investors reading about the deal should also keep in mind that a 2.49% stake does not give Berkshire control, and that the benefits depend on how the reinsurance relationship and joint investments develop over the decade. Neither company has published a target for the business to be ceded, so the practical value is hard to measure from the announcement alone.

More broadly, the deal is part of a trend of cross-border cooperation among large insurers, in which capital and underwriting capabilities are shared through minority stakes and long-term contracts rather than full takeovers. Whether the partnership delivers measurable benefits will become clear in the results Tokio Marine and Berkshire report in coming years.
image_alt: Berkshire Hathaway and Tokio Marine strategic insurance partnership Japan (illustrative)
key_points: On March 23, 2026, Berkshire Hathaway said its subsidiary National Indemnity Company would invest ¥287.4 billion, about $1.8 billion, for a 2.49% strategic stake in Tokio Marine Holdings.

Berkshire will buy about $1.8 billion of Tokio Marine treasury stock, and Tokio Marine will then buy back the same dollar amount of its existing shares; further purchases would likely be on the open market.
Berkshire agreed not to exceed a 9.9% holding without approval from Tokio Marine's board.

The partnership runs for 10 years, covers reinsurance and global investments including mergers and acquisitions, and for the first five years neither company may enter similar agreements with competitors.
Tokio Marine can use National Indemnity as a reinsurance option for any type of insurance without restriction; a Tokio Marine spokesman said Berkshire proposed the partnership.
why_it_matters: It links Japan's largest property and casualty insurer with one of the world's biggest reinsurers and investors. For Tokio Marine it provides reinsurance capacity and a long-term shareholder; for Berkshire, it extends a growing commitment to Japan.

title: Aviva's First Quarter 2026: General Insurance Premiums Up 19% to £3.4 Billion as Direct Line Joins the Group, Solvency Cover at 171%
summary: Aviva's May 14 trading update shows general insurance premiums up 19%, a group combined operating ratio of 94.1%, wealth net flows up 49% to £3.3 billion and a Solvency II cover ratio of 171% after dividends, buybacks and the end of grandfathering.
description:
Aviva, the British insurer, started 2026 with strong growth in general insurance and in its capital-light wealth business, according to its first-quarter trading update published on May 14. The update, headlined as showing the benefits of a diversified model, gives a detailed picture of a group whose size has changed with the purchase of Direct Line, and whose commercial insurance business is facing softer prices. This article summarises the company's own figures. An earlier version of this article described Direct Line capital synergies as already on track without explaining the amounts, and the figures here are taken directly from the trading update. Aviva's half-year results, published later in the year, are a separate release and are not covered.

Start with general insurance, the insurance of cars, homes and businesses. Group premiums were £3.4 billion, up 19% from £2.9 billion in the first quarter of 2025. The group's undiscounted combined operating ratio, which compares claims and costs with premiums, was 94.1%, an improvement of 2.5 percentage points from 96.6%. A ratio below 100% means an underwriting profit. On a discounted basis, which allows for the time value of claims that will be paid in future, the ratio was 90.0%, against 92.9% a year earlier. Aviva says improvements came in all its markets, supported by rate adequacy and better weather.

The United Kingdom and Ireland is the biggest part of the story. General insurance premiums there rose 26% to £2.5 billion from £2.0 billion. Personal lines, which cover consumers, grew 59%, helped by the Direct Line acquisition, which completed on July 1, 2025, and by growth in the intermediated channel, which means sales through brokers and price comparison sites. Aviva says policies sold through price comparison websites have nearly doubled since the start of 2026. Commercial lines fell 7%, which the company attributes to the rating environment, meaning that prices for business insurance are softening, partly offset by strong customer retention. In Canada, premiums rose 3% in constant currency to £0.9 billion, with personal lines up 4% on rate increases and commercial lines up 1%, helped by scheme wins.

The update shows momentum in wealth and retirement. Wealth net flows, the money coming in minus the money going out, were £3.3 billion, up 49% from £2.3 billion, equivalent to 6% of opening assets on an annualised basis. Workplace net flows grew 71%. Wealth assets under management rose 18% to £233 billion. Retirement sales, however, fell to £1.1 billion from £1.8 billion. Individual annuity sales rose 10% and equity release sales rose 8%, but bulk purchase annuity volumes, which are deals to take over pension schemes' obligations, were £0.6 billion against £1.3 billion a year before. Aviva says it maintained pricing discipline in a competitive market, and year-to-date volume reached £1.1 billion at returns of at least the low teens.

Other lines were mixed. Protection sales were £88 million, down 2%, because individual protection fell after strong prior-period sales ahead of stamp duty changes, while group protection grew. In health insurance, in-force premiums grew 9% and the combined operating ratio stayed in the low 90s, but sales fell 31% to £25 million on lower demand in the consumer and small business channels. Aviva Investors reported net flows of £0.1 billion against an outflow of £0.9 billion a year earlier.

Capital is where the numbers need most explanation. The Solvency II shareholder cover ratio, the main measure of an insurer's financial strength under European-style rules, was 171% at March 31, 2026, down from 180% at the end of 2025. Aviva explains that the ratio was reduced by 15 percentage points in the quarter by the 2025 final dividend of £800 million, the previously announced £350 million share buyback and the end of Solvency II grandfathering on £200 million of Tier 2 debt. Capital generation added 6 points, of which around 2.5 came from favourable market movements. The shareholder capital surplus was £6.1 billion. The leverage ratio was 31.6%, against 30.1% at year end. Liquidity at the centre of the group was £1.3 billion at the end of April.

The Direct Line integration is the next lever. Aviva expects capital synergies from the deal to exceed £350 million by the end of 2026, which would add over 7 points to the cover ratio, and about £150 million had been delivered by the end of 2025. It expects solvency to be above its 160% to 180% target range by the end of the year once these synergies are achieved. The company says cost and capital synergies are still expected, and that integration is on track.

On outlook, Aviva says it is on track for its group targets: operating earnings per share growth of 11% a year compounded from 2025 to 2028, a return on equity above 20% by 2028, and cumulative cash remittances above £7 billion over 2026 to 2028. It targets a combined operating ratio below 94% for UK and Ireland general insurance in 2026, and expects Canada to approach 94%. It aims for £100 million of health operating profit in 2026 and £280 million of wealth operating profit by 2027. Chief executive Amanda Blanc said the company had delivered another quarter of strong trading, building momentum in 2026.

How should readers interpret this? The 19% growth in general insurance is largely the effect of buying Direct Line, so it is not comparable with organic growth. The softer commercial market, with premiums down 7% in the UK, shows that after several years of price increases, competition is returning, a theme also seen in the US market. The fall in the solvency ratio is mostly the result of planned capital returns and a technical change and is not a sign of weakness, though investors will watch whether synergies deliver as expected. This summary reports company figures and is not investment advice.

key_points: Aviva's Q1 2026 trading update of May 14 reports general insurance premiums of £3.4 billion, up 19% from £2.9 billion, and a group undiscounted combined operating ratio of 94.1%, 2.5 points better than 96.6%.
UK and Ireland general insurance premiums rose 26% to £2.5 billion; personal lines grew 59% with Direct Line, while commercial lines fell 7% because of the rating environment.
Wealth net flows rose 49% to £3.3 billion and wealth assets under management rose 18% to £233 billion; retirement sales fell to £1.1 billion from £1.8 billion.

The Solvency II shareholder cover ratio was 171%, down from 180%, after a £800 million final dividend, a £350 million buyback and the end of grandfathering on £200 million of Tier 2 debt, which together reduced it by 15 points.
Direct Line capital synergies are expected to exceed £350 million by year end, adding over 7 points to the ratio, and solvency is expected to be above the 160-180% target range by the end of 2026.
why_it_matters: Aviva is one of Britain's largest insurers and its Direct Line purchase has reshaped the UK motor and home market. The update shows how much of its growth comes from that deal, how soft commercial pricing is, and how capital is being returned.

title: AXA's First Quarter 2026: Revenues Up 6% to €38 Billion, Reinsurance Pulled Back 7% and Solvency II at 211%
summary: AXA's Q1 2026 revenues rose 6% to about €38 billion, with property and casualty up 4% to €21.5 billion and life and health up 8% to €16.5 billion, while AXA XL Reinsurance shrank 7% and the Solvency II ratio stood at 211%.
description:
AXA, the French insurance group, reported a steady first quarter of 2026 in which its core insurance lines grew while it deliberately held back in reinsurance. The figures, published in early May and reported by Insurance Business UK on May 6, show a group aligned, in the words of its chief financial officer Alban de Mailly Nesle, with its organic growth strategy. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article referred to a Capital Markets Day and gave asset management figures that are not in the report, so those have been removed. The only related event mentioned is the presentation of a new strategic plan on September 15, 2026.

At group level, gross written premiums and other revenues rose 6% on a comparable basis to about €38 billion, from €37 billion in the first quarter of 2025. Comparable basis means the figures are adjusted for acquisitions, disposals and exchange rate movements, so the growth reflects the underlying business.

Property and casualty insurance, the largest part of the group, grew 4% to €21.5 billion. Within it, personal lines rose 7% to €7 billion, driven by both volume and rate increases. In Europe, personal lines grew 7%, with price rises in most markets except the United Kingdom and Ireland, where competition is stronger. France rose 8%, helped by direct and agent channels and further rate action. In Asia, Africa and the region AXA calls EME-LATAM, personal lines rose 7%, mainly because of higher average premiums in Türkiye and more volume in Mexico. Commercial lines grew 3% to €13.2 billion. AXA XL Insurance, the group's large commercial and specialty arm, grew 2%, with growth in property and specialty and lower casualty volumes. The French commercial portfolio grew 6%, and Asia, Africa and EME-LATAM grew 10%, helped by pricing in Türkiye.

The notable decline was in reinsurance. AXA XL Reinsurance fell 7% to €1.2 billion. Pricing on renewals was down 4%, and AXA said the fall in business reflected a deliberate focus on profitability. In practice, when reinsurance prices drop after several years of increases, a company that is disciplined writes less business rather than accept prices it considers too low. That is consistent with other reports of softer catastrophe reinsurance pricing, such as the Florida renewals in June, in which risk-adjusted prices fell by roughly 15% to 20%. AXA also said natural catastrophe experience in the quarter was slightly below the pro-rated annual budget, and that its full-year catastrophe load remains about 4.5 points of the combined ratio.

Life and health insurance grew faster than property and casualty. Revenues were up 8% to €16.5 billion. Life premiums rose 8% to €10.5 billion, with unit-linked products, in which the customer bears the investment risk, growing 16%, and general account savings, in which the insurer guarantees returns, growing 9%. The company points to campaigns in Spain, single-premium sales in Japan, capital-light general account products in Italy and individual savings in Switzerland. Protection premiums, which pay out on death or illness, rose 4%. Health premiums rose 8% to €5.9 billion, reflecting favourable pricing in all geographies.

Capital is the other half of the picture. AXA's Solvency II ratio, the European measure of an insurer's capital strength, was 211% at March 31, 2026. That compares with 215% on January 1, 2026 and 224% at the end of 2025. The report says the drop at the start of the year reflected the end of Solvency II grandfathering for certain capital instruments, which reduced the ratio by 10 points. Grandfathering allows older instruments to count towards capital for a limited time, and when it ends, they stop counting. The ratio remains well above the regulatory minimum of 100%, and the Insurance Business article notes that peers such as Allianz, Zurich and Generali have reported Solvency II ratios generally around or above 200%.

For guidance, AXA expects underlying earnings per share growth for 2026 at the upper end of its 6% to 8% target range, assuming no significant deterioration in operating, pricing or market conditions. It plans to present a new strategic plan covering 2027 to 2029 on September 15, 2026.

What does the quarter tell us? First, personal insurance pricing is still rising in many European markets, but not in the United Kingdom and Ireland, which matches Aviva's experience of intense competition in the UK. Second, commercial insurance is growing slowly, and the casualty line is being managed down at AXA XL, reflecting caution about liability claims. Third, savings and health are increasing faster than the property and casualty business, which suggests that the group is benefiting from structural demand for retirement saving and healthcare cover.

There are limits to a quarterly update. It reports revenues and not profit, and it does not give the combined ratio for the quarter, so readers cannot judge underwriting profitability from it. Investors typically wait for half-year results for earnings figures. This summary reports published figures and is not investment advice.
image_alt: AXA France insurance group quarterly revenue results 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: AXA reported Q1 2026 gross written premiums and other revenues up 6% on a comparable basis to €38 billion, from €37 billion a year earlier.

Property and casualty rose 4% to €21.5 billion: personal lines +7% to €7 billion, commercial lines +3% to €13.2 billion, while AXA XL Reinsurance fell 7% to €1.2 billion as renewal pricing was down 4%.
Life and health revenues rose 8% to €16.5 billion; life premiums rose 8% to €10.5 billion, with unit-linked products up 16%, and health premiums rose 8% to €5.9 billion.

The Solvency II ratio was 211% at March 31, 2026, down from 215% on January 1 and 224% at end-2025; the end of grandfathering on some capital instruments cut the ratio by 10 points at the start of the year.
AXA expects underlying earnings per share growth at the upper end of its 6-8% target range and will present its 2027-2029 strategic plan on September 15, 2026.
why_it_matters: AXA is one of Europe's largest insurers, so its quarter shows where demand and pricing are headed in personal, commercial and life insurance. The decision to shrink reinsurance, where prices were falling, signals a profit-over-growth approach across the sector.

title: Swiss Re Institute: Secondary Perils Caused a Record 92% of 2025's $107 Billion in Insured Catastrophe Losses, and a Trend Year Would Cost $148 Billion
summary: Swiss Re Institute's sigma report says insured natural catastrophe losses were $107 billion in 2025, with wildfires, storms and floods driving a record 92%, and that a return to trend would put 2026 losses near $148 billion.
description:
Natural disasters cost insurers $107 billion in 2025, according to the Swiss Re Institute's annual sigma catastrophe study, and almost all of that came from the kinds of events insurers once treated as minor. The Institute reports that secondary perils, a category that includes wildfires, severe convective storms and floods, made up a record 92% of the global insured natural catastrophe losses. This article is based on Swiss Re's press release for the study and on the summary on the Institute's own website. An earlier version of this article described the wildfire growth rate as about 12% a year and gave a figure of $320 billion as a projection. The press release gives 14% for North American wildfire losses and presents $320 billion only as a modelled peak scenario, so the text has been corrected.

The headline figures are as follows. Insured losses from natural catastrophes were $107 billion. Economic losses, which include uninsured damage, were $220 billion, and about 49% of these were insured, the highest insured share in the history of the sigma series. Adding man-made losses of $13 billion brings total insured losses to $120 billion, and total economic losses to $235 billion, compared with $338 billion in 2024 and a previous ten-year average of $280 billion. In other words, 2025 was cheaper than 2024 on every measure, but Swiss Re cautions against reading too much into that.

The reason for caution is stated by Balz Grollimund, the Institute's head of catastrophe perils. He said the relatively low losses reflected favourable variability rather than any easing of underlying risk. The page on the Institute's website adds that the long-term trend would imply about $140 billion for 2025, so the actual outcome came in below it. One important piece of luck was the absence of a major hurricane landfall in the United States in 2025. Tropical cyclones are the largest contributor to long-term average losses, so a year without one produces a lower total.

The perils that did cause losses were secondary perils. The Los Angeles wildfires of January 2025 cost about $40 billion in combined insured losses, the largest insured wildfire loss event in sigma records. Severe convective storms, which include hail, tornadoes and thunderstorm wind, caused $51 billion, the third-costliest year on record for that peril after 2023 and 2024 when measured in 2025 prices. Flood losses were relatively small, at $3.4 billion against a previous five-year average of $15.4 billion. Together, wildfires, severe convective storms and floods caused 88% of the global insured natural catastrophe losses, while the 92% figure covers all secondary perils.

The study looks at why losses keep rising. Swiss Re says long-term insured natural catastrophe losses grow at a rate of 5% to 7% a year. Exposure growth, meaning more and more valuable property in areas at risk, explains more than 80% of the long-term global increase in weather-related insured losses between 1970 and 2025. Severe convective storms account for 38% of the growth in historical losses, wildfires for about 20% despite having the highest growth rates, and floods for roughly 10%. Jérôme Jean Haegeli, who heads the Institute and is the group's chief economist, summarised the problem by saying that more valuable property is being built in harm's way, and rebuilding costs have risen.

Regional patterns differ. In North America, the growth in losses is driven mainly by wildfires and severe convective storms, and the Institute says insured wildfire losses grow at 14% a year, as longer fire seasons and changes in temperature and rainfall add to the threat. In Europe, over half of the growth in insured losses comes from severe convective storms, growing at about 10% a year, and less than half of that increase is explained by exposure growth, which suggests that storm characteristics and vulnerability are changing. In Asia, the growth in secondary-peril losses is dominated by floods. In Oceania, severe convective storms and floods share the growth more evenly, and wildfires play a smaller part.

For 2026, Swiss Re gives two reference points. If losses return to the normal long-term trend, insured losses would be $148 billion. In the modelled peak-loss scenario, which represents a severe year and not a forecast, losses could reach about $320 billion. The Institute stresses that its trend figure is not a prediction of what will happen. Urs Baertschi, who runs property and casualty reinsurance at Swiss Re, noted that the company protects against peak risks by absorbing low-frequency, high-severity events, which is the function of reinsurance.

There is also a gap between damage and protection. In emerging economies, typically 80% to 90% of catastrophe losses are uninsured. When a disaster strikes in a country with low insurance penetration, the cost falls on households, businesses and governments instead of insurers. Swiss Re recommends sustained and well-designed adaptation and risk mitigation to maintain insurability and affordability, identifying the drivers of rising losses so that risks can be managed before losses occur, and pairing stronger risk management with broader and more accessible insurance in emerging economies.

What does this mean for ordinary readers? Property insurance prices reflect the expected cost of events like these, so rising catastrophe losses are one reason premiums for homes in wildfire, hail and flood areas keep increasing. Measures that reduce damage, such as fire-resistant roofing, defensible space around homes, hail-resistant materials and flood barriers, matter for insurers as well as for owners, because they can improve availability and prices. For governments, building codes and land-use decisions determine how much exposure grows. The study makes the case that insurance, adaptation and planning have to work together, because none of them is sufficient alone.

Readers who want the full numbers can consult the complete sigma report on Swiss Re's website. The percentages and totals above are Swiss Re's estimates, and different organisations use different methods and definitions, so figures from other catastrophe analysts may differ.
image_alt: Natural catastrophe wildfire storm flood insured losses 2025 Swiss Re sigma (illustrative)
key_points: Swiss Re Institute says global insured natural catastrophe losses were $107 billion in 2025, with secondary perils such as wildfires, severe convective storms and floods causing a record 92%.

The January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires produced about $40 billion of insured losses, the largest insured wildfire event in sigma records; severe convective storms cost $51 billion, the third-costliest year on record.
Economic natural catastrophe losses were $220 billion, about 49% of them insured, the highest insured share on sigma record; total insured losses including man-made events were $120 billion.

Long-term insured losses grow 5-7% a year, and exposure growth explains more than 80% of the rise in weather-related insured losses between 1970 and 2025; wildfire losses in North America grow about 14% a year.
If losses follow the long-term trend, 2026 would bring $148 billion; in a modelled peak scenario they could reach about $320 billion.
why_it_matters: Insured disaster losses shape property insurance prices and availability. The report argues that 2025 was a lucky year, not a safer one, and that building more valuable property in harm's way keeps pushing the long-term costs up.

title: Berkshire's Ajit Jain on Insuring Ships in the Strait of Hormuz: 'The Short Answer Is It Depends on the Price'
summary: At Berkshire Hathaway's May 2026 annual meeting, Ajit Jain said the company has taken a small participation in a Hormuz shipping insurance program but has written no deals, pending underwriting terms including US Navy escort assurances.
description:
Insuring ships through a war zone is a question of price, according to one of the world's most respected insurance executives. At Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting in 2026, Ajit Jain, who runs the company's insurance operations, was asked when Berkshire could insure ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz. His reply was that the short answer is that it depends on the price. The remark was reported by Claims Journal on May 5, 2026, and by Carrier Management two days earlier. This article summarises that report and adds details of the government-backed programme from a later Insurance Business report. An earlier version of this article described the programme and its partners as part of Jain's remarks. The Claims Journal report does not mention the programme's size or its partners, so those details are now attributed to the later report.

Here is what Jain said, according to the report. He drew a comparison with Warren Buffett's answer on pandemic coverage at the 2020 meeting, when the topic was a different risk. He said demand for insurance for ships stalled by the war with Iran is high, but that there is enough capacity in the insurance world that would like to write that risk. He attributed the capacity to insurers with surplus capital looking for places to deploy it. In other words, the constraint is not a lack of willing insurers. It is that the terms have to make sense.

Berkshire's own position is limited. Jain said the company has taken a small participation in a programme set up to insure ships in the Strait, but the article gives no size for that stake. Berkshire has not written any deals yet. He said the company is still fine-tuning the underwriting terms, including assurances that the US Navy will escort the ships. Berkshire has set a price at which it would be comfortable underwriting the risk, but, in his words, nothing has happened as yet. The article does not state the price.

What is the programme? A later article by Insurance Business, published on June 28, 2026, gives more detail on the war-risk market. It says that the conflict began on February 28, 2026, and that in early March the US International Development Finance Corporation launched a $20 billion maritime reinsurance facility. On April 3 the facility was expanded to $40 billion. Chubb was the lead underwriter, and other participants were Travelers, Liberty Mutual, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, Starr and CNA. The US government assumes half of the risk, or $20 billion, and the seven participating insurers back the other half. That structure explains Jain's comment about price and escorts: a government backstop reduces the risk for private insurers, but they still want assurance about the conditions of each voyage.

How high have war-risk premiums gone? The Insurance Business article says the pre-conflict war-risk rate for Hormuz transits was about 0.25% of a ship's hull value. At the peak, it was as high as 10%, an increase of close to 4,000%, according to Dylan Saunders-Mortimer of Marsh. Current estimates at the time of writing were 3% to 8%, which equals $3 million to $8 million for a single large tanker transit. The Joint War Committee of the Lloyd's Market Association expanded its high-risk designation to cover the entire Persian Gulf. A ceasefire signed earlier in June was undermined by renewed hostilities on June 27, according to the article. Because conditions are changing, readers should check current news for the latest status.

Other voices in that article put Jain's remark in context. Rahul Kapoor of S&P Global Energy said transits are being avoided because of the safety of the crew, cargo and vessel and not insurance alone. Neeraj Gupta of Policybazaar UAE said underwriters need two to four weeks of confirmed de-escalation before lower risk feeds into pricing, and that a full return to pre-conflict rates could take several months. Rishi Thapar of Lockton said the market is stabilising but not resetting. The article says traffic through the Strait had fallen about 95% from a pre-conflict average of 178 ships per day, citing Khaleej Times.

What does this say about insurance more broadly? War risk is usually excluded from standard policies and is bought separately, at short notice, for specific voyages. It is a classic case in which private insurers will cover a risk only at a price that reflects extreme uncertainty. Government-backed facilities, like the one described, have precedents in terrorism and political risk insurance, where governments share extreme losses. The Hormuz case is a test of how effective such facilities are at restoring trade when ship owners and crews are concerned about physical safety.

For readers outside the industry, the practical effect is on shipping costs and energy supply chains. Higher insurance costs are passed on in freight rates and can ultimately affect prices, although the Insurance Business article says transits are being limited by safety as much as by insurance. Jain's remark is a reminder that capital exists to take the risk if the price is right, and that the price is set by information about the likelihood of attack, which changes with each event.
source_name: Claims Journal / Carrier Management (Berkshire annual meeting) and Insurance Business
image_alt: Berkshire Hathaway Ajit Jain marine insurance Hormuz Strait risk underwriting (illustrative)
key_points: Asked at Berkshire Hathaway's 2026 annual meeting when it could insure ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz, Ajit Jain said: 'The short answer is it depends on the price.'

Jain said Berkshire has taken a small participation in a program set up to insure ships in the Strait but had not written any deals, and was still fine-tuning terms including assurances that the US Navy will escort ships.
He said demand is high but 'there's enough capacity in the insurance world today that would like to write that risk', from insurers with surplus capital looking for places to deploy it.

Later reporting by Insurance Business (June 28) says the US International Development Finance Corporation launched a $20 billion maritime reinsurance facility in early March, expanded to $40 billion on April 3, with Chubb as lead underwriter.
That reporting lists Travelers, Liberty Mutual, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, Starr and CNA as participants, with the US government taking half of the risk and the seven insurers the other half.
why_it_matters: Shipping through Hormuz depends on insurance as much as on ships. How Berkshire and other insurers price this risk shows whether war-risk cover can return at levels that let trade move, and how governments can back the market when private insurers hesitate.

title: Fitch: Florida's Reinsurance Market Is Better Placed for the 2026 Hurricane Season, but Single-State Insurers Remain More Exposed
summary: Fitch says early indications put Florida reinsurance pricing down roughly 15% to 20% risk-adjusted, with insurers seeking an extra $5 billion to $7 billion of cover, Citizens down to about 295,000 policies and discipline expected to hold.
description:
Florida's property insurance market enters the 2026 hurricane season in better shape than in recent years, according to a commentary by Fitch Ratings reported by the reinsurance news site Artemis on June 10, 2026. The credit rating agency says that conditions favour Florida insurers as they buy reinsurance, with more capacity, lower prices and more flexible terms, but it also warns that results will depend on whether storms make landfall. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article gave a 2025 combined ratio, a surplus growth figure, a count of 21 new insurers and a catastrophe bond total as Fitch's statements. The Artemis report of the Fitch commentary does not contain those figures, which come from a different broker report, so they have been removed here.

Start with pricing. Fitch says that early indications suggest risk-adjusted pricing is down by roughly 15% to 20% across many layers of reinsurance programmes. Risk-adjusted means that the figure takes account of changes in the risk covered. Fitch notes that these are early indications for the June and July 2026 renewals, so final outcomes could differ. A separate broker review, which we have covered in our report on the June renewals, reached a similar range.

Demand is also growing. Florida insurers were expected to seek an additional $5 billion to $7 billion of reinsurance at mid-year. Fitch lists several reasons: exposure growth, rising insured values, the depopulation of Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, the formation of new carriers, and shifting attachment points for the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund, the state's reinsurance programme. Some of the demand is concentrated below the FHCF layer. When insurers buy more cover and the supply of capacity is plentiful, prices fall, which is what is happening.

Citizens is central to the picture. It is the state-backed insurer of last resort, and its policy count has fallen sharply. According to Fitch, policies in force peaked at about 1.4 million in 2023 and had fallen to roughly 295,000 by April 2026. Fitch expects further reductions to slow, because the opportunities for private insurers to take policies out of Citizens are shrinking. As Citizens shrinks, the risk it held has moved to private insurers, which then need reinsurance.

The weather outlook matters too. Early 2026 forecasts point to a slightly below-average Atlantic hurricane season, and the 2025 season had no US hurricane landfalls. Fitch notes that neutral conditions in the El Niño-Southern Oscillation are likely to shift towards El Niño over the next several months, which tends to suppress Atlantic hurricane activity. These are forecasts and carry uncertainty; a below-average season can still include a damaging storm.

On capacity, Fitch says conditions favour Florida cedents, the insurers that buy reinsurance, heading into the June and July renewals, with more capacity from traditional reinsurers and from insurance-linked securities markets. Strong catastrophe bond issuance and broader third-party capital are supporting capacity, though Fitch does not quantify either. Reinsurance buyers with nationwide US programmes are seeing similar improvements. Cedents are using the savings to buy additional protection, and terms have become more flexible. Protection is available across more of the programme tower, with better access in some lower layers, and alternative capital is adding competitive pressure at higher attachment points.

Will discipline hold? Fitch expects reinsurers to maintain discipline and rate adequacy, citing high catastrophe risk and climate concerns. It says some terms have relaxed, but structures are holding, and that attachment points are not falling without buyers paying more for them. In other words, reinsurers are giving some price relief but not unlimited access to their capital.

The risk is concentrated in smaller companies. Fitch says insurers operating solely in Florida may be more susceptible than larger national carriers in a heavy catastrophe year, because their capital reserves are typically thinner and their risk is not diversified across states. It adds that pricing and capacity could become more volatile after a major catastrophe event. That caution is important for policyholders as well: a small insurer that fails after a hurricane can leave customers needing new cover, with claims handled by the state guaranty association.

Fitch credits legislative reform, growth in private-market capacity and better reinsurance conditions since 2023 with strengthening the market. Loss outcomes, it stresses, will still depend on whether storms make landfall and how severe they are.

What does this mean for homeowners? Cheaper reinsurance reduces insurers' costs and can ease pressure for rate increases, but it does not make prices fall automatically, and rates must also reflect claims, rebuilding costs and each company's own financial position. Policyholders should check the financial strength rating of their insurer, compare quotes, review wind and flood coverage and prepare for the season regardless of the forecast. The commentary is an assessment by a rating agency and not a guarantee of results, and readers should treat the quoted percentages as early indications that renewal outcomes can change.
image_alt: Florida hurricane season 2026 insurance reinsurance market positioning (illustrative)
key_points: Fitch's commentary, reported by Artemis on June 10, 2026, says early indications show risk-adjusted Florida reinsurance pricing down roughly 15% to 20% across many layers.

Florida insurers were expected to seek an additional $5 billion to $7 billion of reinsurance at mid-year, driven by exposure growth, higher insured values, Citizens depopulation, new carriers and shifting FHCF attachment points.
Citizens policies in force peaked at about 1.4 million in 2023 and fell to roughly 295,000 by April 2026; Fitch expects further reductions to slow.
Early 2026 forecasts point to a slightly below-average Atlantic hurricane season, the 2025 season had no US hurricane landfalls, and conditions may shift towards El Niño.

Fitch expects reinsurers to keep discipline, warns that Florida-only insurers may be more susceptible in a heavy catastrophe year, and says pricing and capacity could become more volatile after a major event.
why_it_matters: Reinsurance costs flow through to what Florida homeowners pay, and the state's insurers depend on it. Fitch's view is that conditions are favourable for buyers, but that a single major hurricane could change the picture quickly.

title: BIBA Launches an Accredited Cyber Insurance Broker Directory to Point UK Small Businesses to Specialists, Citing a Gap in Cover
summary: The British Insurance Brokers' Association says only 10% of UK businesses and 5% of charities hold a specific cyber policy, according to the government's latest survey; its directory lists brokers who meet cyber-security, insurance and training criteria developed with input from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology.
description:
Most small British businesses do not have insurance against cyber attacks, and the trade body for insurance brokers has launched a directory aimed at changing that. The British Insurance Brokers' Association (BIBA) has set up the BIBA Accredited Cyber Insurance Broker Directory, which allows a business to search for a broker that has met a defined set of standards for cyber expertise. The facts below come from BIBA's own press release, whose page was updated on July 14, 2026, and from trade coverage including The Insurer, which reported the plan on January 19, 2026. BIBA's pages carry several dates, including announcements in January and May 2026, and the release says it was announced at the BIBA Conference without giving the date, so we cannot give a single launch date. The release does not say how many brokers are accredited.

Why was it created? The press release says the aim is to help protect UK businesses, to raise awareness of cyber insurance and to narrow the protection gap by connecting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) with genuine expertise. BIBA's chief executive, Graeme Trudgill, described the aim as 'ensuring SMEs can be signposted to a genuine expert'. He also said 'Cyber threats are on the increase and this is a positive initiative'. The protection gap is the difference between the losses businesses face and the amount covered by insurance. The release uses government survey data to illustrate it: DSIT's latest survey found that 10% of businesses and 5% of charities hold a specific cyber insurance policy. The release does not give the date or sample of that survey, so readers should treat the percentages as the figures BIBA chose to quote.

What do brokers have to do to be accredited? According to the release, accredited brokers must run their own cyber security framework that generally meets or exceeds Cyber Essentials, the UK government-backed baseline certification for basic security controls. They must hold standalone cyber insurance for their own business. Their relevant staff must complete continuous cyber training and have a good understanding of cyber risks. The process, BIBA says, was developed by the association and informed by industry views and government guidelines. The idea is that a broker who has secured and insured their own firm is better placed to advise a client on doing the same.

What is the government's role? Some summaries describe the directory as a formal partnership with DSIT, the department responsible for UK cyber policy. The release is more limited: it says BIBA engaged with DSIT while developing the accreditation criteria, and it includes a quote from Baroness Lloyd of Effra, the Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for the digital economy, who said, 'This work matters – and we need to keep pushing it further.' That is support for the initiative, but the release does not say that the department runs, funds or endorses the directory in a formal sense, so we describe the relationship as engagement.

How serious is the threat to small firms? BIBA quotes two sources. The Hiscox Cyber Readiness Report 2025 found that 59% of respondents had experienced a cyber-attack in the previous 12 months. A buyers' guide produced by BIBA with the insurer CFC shows that SMEs are targeted nearly four times as often as large organisations. Both are survey and industry findings, and the release does not say how they were measured. They are offered as context for why advice matters: small firms are attacked often but may lack both the specialist knowledge to buy suitable cover and the budget to cope with an attack on their own.

How does a business use it? A business can search the directory on the BIBA website for an accredited broker, and brokers can apply for accreditation through the same site. BIBA says the directory will be promoted in its 'Ben the Broker' advertising campaign, which suggests the association wants consumers and firms to find it. The directory does not sell insurance itself. It points to intermediaries who can assess a company's cyber risk, recommend a structure of cover and help with measures to reduce the risk. An accredited broker still has to be judged on its own merits, as accreditation is a baseline and not a guarantee of price, claims service or suitability.

What should a small business do now? The practical steps are to check which controls it already has, such as multi-factor authentication, regular backups and staff training, because insurers usually ask about them. Then to ask a broker whether the policy covers ransomware, business interruption, data restoration and liability to customers, and what the exclusions and the limits are. Policy wording differs between insurers, so reading the wording carefully matters. The directory is a starting point, not a recommendation of any one broker. This article is a news summary and not insurance advice.

why_it_matters: Many small firms have no cyber policy and do not know who to ask, so they carry the whole cost of a ransomware or fraud incident themselves. A directory built on stated standards is an attempt to close that gap by making it easier to find a broker who understands the risk.
